newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices steady in pause before OPEC talks.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices steady in pause before OPEC talks.

text.p: World oil prices steadied on Thursday with traders reluctant to second guess the market ahead of next week's OPEC ministerial meeting in Vienna.
Dealers decided it was time to take a breather after data released on Wednesday indicating that U.S. gasoline production was at record levels caused prices to slide.
"It's a consolidative day, we're trading inside Wednesday's range on crude...but I think there's some feeling that things were overdone on the downside yesterday," a broker said.
London August futures for world benchmark Brent blend crude closed unchanged at $17.77 a barrel.
Prices fell to a 13-month low last week but staged a recovery before taking another hit on Wednesday as large investment funds baled out.
Market watchers said recent market volatility meant that traders were undecided whether to take "long" or "short" positions before OPEC oil ministers convene their meeting on June 25.

"Most people feel like whirling dervishes, one minute they think they should be long, the next short, they're getting burnt all the time...the market's so choppy," said Charles Gray of brokerage Prudential Bache.

Despite a $7-a-barrel tumble in oil prices since the start of the year, market watchers were not expecting the 11-member OPEC cartel to meddle with its 25.03 million barrel per day (bpd) supply quota.
But some firm action on quota busting is on the agenda, they said.

In the shorter term, the market's bearish backdrop of brimming U.S. gasoline tanks was countered by slow progress towards the resumption of Iraqi crude exports under the United Nations oil-for-food plan.
Reports that Britain and the United States were seeking to impose new sanctions on Iraq for blocking U.N. weapons inspection teams several times this month also helped support prices.

The new measures would include preventing Iraqi officials from travelling abroad and suspending reviews of trade sanctions until Baghdad cooperates, according to a draft resolution obtained by Reuters.
An Iraqi diplomat at the United Nations in New York said on Wednesday Baghdad would not resume oil sales until money raised in Iraq's first six months of oil sales had all been spent.
Some $800 million of the $2 billion raised in Iraqi sales in six months to June cannot be spent until aid contracts are approved.
Although the second term of the humanitarian agreement officially got underway on June 8, some traders are not expecting the oil sales under the second plan until August.
"It looks like it's going to be hold up after hold up. I don't think anyone's thinking the oil is round the corner," said one.
